problem_text: A magician intends to perform the following trick. She announces a positive integer n, along with 2n real numbers x_1 < ... < x_{2n}, to the audience. A member of the audience then secretly chooses a polynomial P(x) of degree n with real coefficients, computes the 2n values P(x_1), ..., P(x_{2n}), and writes down these 2n values on the blackboard in non-decreasing order. After that the magician announces the secret polynomial to the audience. Can the magician find a strategy to perform such a trick?
solution_text: The answer is No. For any choice of n and x_1 < ... < x_{2n}, consider any non-identity permutation sigma of {1, ..., 2n}. We seek two distinct degree-n polynomials P and Q such that Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) for all i. P has n+1 coefficients and Q has n+1 coefficients, giving 2n+2 unknowns. The equations Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) provide 2n linear constraints. The solution space therefore has dimension at least 2. After normalizing (e.g., fixing the leading coefficient of P), the dimension is at least 1, guaranteeing non-trivial solutions with both P and Q of degree n. For a non-identity permutation sigma, P != Q generically (since Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) != P(x_i) for some i). The sorted multisets {P(x_1), ..., P(x_{2n})} and {Q(x_1), ..., Q(x_{2n})} are identical by construction. Hence the magician sees the same sorted values from two different polynomials and cannot distinguish them. Therefore no strategy exists for any n.
solution_summary: For any non-identity permutation sigma, the system Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) has 2n equations in 2n+2 unknowns (coefficients of P and Q), so non-trivial solutions exist with distinct degree-n polynomials P != Q producing identical sorted value multisets. The magician cannot distinguish them, so no strategy exists.

rounds.question: Describe the structure of this problem. What information does the magician know, what is lost when the values are sorted, and what must the magician recover?
rounds.expected_answer: The magician knows n and the ordered reals x_1 < ... < x_{2n}. The audience picks a degree-n polynomial P and evaluates it at all 2n points, then sorts the values in non-decreasing order. The sorting destroys the pairing between each value and its corresponding x_i. The magician must recover the polynomial P from the sorted multiset of values alone.

rounds.question: List all possible approaches to determine whether the magician can always succeed. Include approaches that look for counterexamples.
rounds.expected_answer: Possible approaches: (1) Try small cases like n=1 to see if the magician can determine P. (2) Attempt to construct a strategy using interpolation or other methods. (3) Look for counterexamples — find two different degree-n polynomials that produce the same sorted multiset. (4) Use a permutation argument: if a non-identity permutation sigma can map P's values to Q's values, then P and Q are indistinguishable. (5) Use dimension counting to show such P and Q must exist.

rounds.question: Try n=1 specifically: given two sorted values from a degree-1 polynomial evaluated at x_1 < x_2, can two different lines produce the same sorted pair?
rounds.expected_answer: For n=1, P(x) = ax + b. The values P(x_1) and P(x_2) are sorted. If a > 0, the sorted pair is {P(x_1), P(x_2)}; if a < 0, it is {P(x_2), P(x_1)}. Given sorted values {v_1, v_2} with v_1 < v_2, there are two possibilities: an increasing line with P(x_1)=v_1, P(x_2)=v_2, or a decreasing line with P(x_1)=v_2, P(x_2)=v_1. These are two different degree-1 polynomials. So n=1 fails — the magician cannot determine P.

rounds.question: For general n, consider a non-identity permutation sigma of {1,...,2n}. Set up the system Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) for all i. Count the unknowns (coefficients of P and Q) versus the number of equations. What does the dimension of the solution space tell you?
rounds.expected_answer: P has n+1 coefficients and Q has n+1 coefficients, giving 2n+2 unknowns total. The equations Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) for i=1,...,2n give 2n linear equations. The solution space has dimension at least 2n+2 - 2n = 2. After normalizing (e.g., fixing the leading coefficient of P to 1), the dimension is at least 1, guaranteeing non-trivial solutions. For a non-identity permutation sigma, P and Q are generically distinct (Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) != P(x_i) for some i). Both can be chosen to have degree exactly n.

rounds.question: Connect the dimension argument to the conclusion: if P != Q produce the same sorted multiset of values, what does this imply about any strategy the magician might use?
rounds.expected_answer: If P and Q are distinct degree-n polynomials with Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) for a non-identity permutation sigma, then the sorted multisets {P(x_1),...,P(x_{2n})} and {Q(x_1),...,Q(x_{2n})} are identical by construction. The magician sees the same sorted values from two different polynomials. No strategy can distinguish P from Q, because the input (sorted values) is identical. Since this works for any n and any choice of x_i, no universal strategy exists.

rounds.question: Summarize the complete proof and state the final answer.
rounds.expected_answer: The answer is No. For any positive integer n and any x_1 < ... < x_{2n}, pick any non-identity permutation sigma. The system Q(x_i) = P(x_{sigma(i)}) has 2n equations in 2n+2 unknowns (the coefficients of P and Q), so the solution space has dimension at least 2. Non-trivial solutions exist with both P and Q of degree n and P != Q. These produce identical sorted value multisets, so the magician cannot uniquely determine the polynomial. Therefore no strategy exists for any n.
